payload.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Full Bench held that when a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is established, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award to the third party and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.
payload.ratio: Pursuant to the mandate of Section 149(1) and (4) of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party judgment or award as a judgment debtor and recover the amount from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.

pay and recovery concept. However, prior to and even after Swaran Singh's case, the apex Court in
some cases, as discussed, exercised its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 142 of the
Constitution and directed the insurer to satisfy the award of the Tribunal and recover the amount
from the insured, even after coming to the conclusion that there was no liability on the part of the
insurer but in order to uphold the main object of Section 149(1) and 149(2) of the Act, particularly in
Shamanna's case and subsequent rulings of the apex court. Though there are divergent decisions of
the apex Court both prior to and after the decision in Swaran Singh, we find there is a strong,
continuous, consistency in following the principles laid down by the apex Court in Swaran Singh's
case which is of a larger Bench compared to all other Benches subsequent to it, particularly the
principles with reference to the concept of pay and recovery.

Oriental Insurance Company Limited and others, has also in fact, dealt with various earlier
decisions of the Apex Court with reference to the principle of pay and recover and the law has been
summarized in the said case. The apex Court after discussing Sections 147, 149 and 168 of the Act
held that in case of a third party, award passed against the owner has to be paid by the insurer and
recovered from the insured.
53(a). In the aforesaid case, the apex court has dealt with the principle of pay and recovery and
summarized the law by relying upon Swaran Singh wherein the apex Court has considered as to
whether the Supreme Court alone has got jurisdiction to order for pay and recover by exercising the
extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution of India or whether the Tribunal and
the High Courts have also got such power to order for pay and recovery. The apex court relying upon
Swaran Singh's case and also Laxminarayan Dhut's case, as already referred to above by us in this
judgment, has reiterated that the decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other
than third party risks. But, in the case of third party risks, the insurer has to indemnify the amount
and if so directed to recover the same from the insured. The Hon'ble Supreme Court also relied upon

fundamental and which has contributed to the cause of accident, the Tribunal can interpret the

with sub Section (7) of section 149 of the Act, the Tribunal can direct that the insurer make the
payment and recover the same from the insured, which, it has been compelled to pay to third party
under the award by the Tribunal.

60. Therefore, sub Section (4) and (5) of Section 149 of the Act are enumerated as special
contingencies where the statute itself provides the insurer to recover the amount paid under the
award by it from the insured. Apart from that, the apex Court has observed that, under Section
149(2) of the Act, despite the defence taken by the insurer so far as the fundamental breach of
conditions are concerned, then also the Tribunal can order for 'pay and recovery'. But, it all depends
upon the facts and circumstance of each case, where the Tribunal has to consider each and every

args.question: Which judgments apply the 'pay and recover' principle, and in what circumstances?
args.answer:
## Judgments Applying the 'Pay and Recover' Principle

The 'pay and recover' principle (also called 'pay and recovery') directs an insurer to pay compensation to a third-party claimant first, and then recover that amount from the insured owner/driver. It arises from the statutory scheme under Sections 149(1), (4) and (5) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, as interpreted by the Supreme Court in *Swaran Singh* and subsequent cases.

Below are the judgments from the corpus that apply or discuss this principle, organised by the circumstances in which it arises.

---

### A. BREACH OF POLICY CONDITIONS — DRIVING LICENCE DEFECTS

This is the most common application. Where the insurer proves a breach of policy conditions (especially a defective driving licence), the insurer is still directed to pay the third party and recover from the insured.

| Doc ID | Case Name | Circumstance |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| **doc_024** | *Sunil Shreesail Killiket v. Subbraya* (MACT, Bengaluru, 2024) | Driver lacked a valid driving licence altogether. Tribunal held this was a fundamental breach but directed insurer to pay the third-party claimant first and recover from the owner. |
| **doc_027** | *The Manager v. Chennamma* (Madras HC, 2013) | Driver held only an LMV licence without the specific endorsement to drive a heavy goods vehicle. Insurer directed to pay and recover. The court also laid down the *Nanjappan* mode of recovery (execution proceedings without a separate suit). |
| **doc_035** | *United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. V. Vijayakumar* (Madras HC, 2010) | Driver of a transport vehicle held only an LMV licence without the badge/authorisation required for transport vehicles. Insurer directed to pay and recover. |
| **doc_003** | *United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Parvathi Hebbar* (Karnataka HC, 2017) | Driving licence had expired and was renewed more than 30 days later — the renewal operated only from the date of renewal, not retrospectively. Insurer directed to pay and recover. |
| **doc_001** | *United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Neelam Devi* (P&H HC, 2023) | Driver lacked a special endorsement for transporting hazardous/dangerous goods under the CMV Rules. Insurer granted pay-and-recover rights. |
| **doc_033** | *Satto & Ors v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd.* (Delhi HC, 2013) | Invalid driving licence. The court held the insurer's liability to satisfy the third-party award is **statutory** — it must pay first and recover from the owner/driver. |
| **doc_025** | *New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Yallavva* (Karnataka HC Full Bench, 2020) | **Leading Full Bench decision.** Held that even where a fundamental breach under Section 149(2) is proved, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured. This applies to both 'Act' policies and contractual policies. Also confirmed that **Tribunals and High Courts** (not just the Supreme Court under Article 142) have the power to order pay-and-recover. |

---

### B. PASSENGERS IN GOODS VEHICLES — DISCRETIONARY APPLICATION

| Doc ID | Case Name | Circumstance |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| **doc_026** | *National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Ellappa* (Madras HC, 2009) | Passengers in a goods vehicle. The court held that since Section 147 does not statutorily require coverage of passengers in goods vehicles, pay-and-recover is **not ipso facto** applicable. However, the appellate court may **discretionarily** apply it depending on facts — here, given the claimants' poverty and prolonged litigation (since 1996), the court directed pay-and-recover. |

---

### C. WHERE PAY-AND-RECOVER WAS REFUSED (LIMITING PRECEDENTS)

These judgments hold that pay-and-recover **cannot** be ordered in certain situations:

| Doc ID | Case Name | Circumstance & Reasoning |
|--------|-----------|--------------------------|
| **doc_028** | *United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Sukumarbai Nikam* (Bombay HC, 2019) | **Private vehicle used for hire/reward.** Deceased was a passenger in a private jeep hired for a wedding — this was a breach of policy conditions. The court held such a passenger is **not a 'third party'** under the Act policy, and the Tribunal cannot invoke pay-and-recover. Insurer completely exonerated. |
| **doc_029** | *United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Minor Mahesh Kanubhai* (Gujarat HC, 2014) | **Gratuitous passengers in a goods vehicle/tractor.** Where the risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the policy, Sections 149(4) and (5) are not attracted. Neither the Tribunal nor the High Court has power to direct pay-and-recover. |
| **doc_030** | *Dadapeera v. Mallesh* (Karnataka HC, 2025) | **Person travelling on tractor mud-guard.** This violates Regulation 28 of the Rules of the Road Regulations. Such a person is not a 'third party' entitled to the statutory benefit of pay-and-recover. Insurer exonerated; owner directed to pay. |

---

### D. KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES FROM THE CORPUS

1. **Statutory basis**: The principle flows from Sections 149(1), (4) and (5) of the MV Act. The insurer's liability to pay the third party is statutory and arises from the mere issuance of a certificate of insurance (*Satto*, doc_033; *Yallavva*, doc_025).

2. **Tribunals have the power**: Contrary to earlier doubts that only the Supreme Court under Article 142 could order pay-and-recover, the Full Bench in *Yallavva* (doc_025) and the Madras HC in *Chennamma* (doc_027) confirmed that Tribunals and High Courts possess this power.

3. **Mode of recovery**: Per *Oriental Insurance Co. v. Nanjappan* (cited in doc_027), the insurer need not file a separate suit — it can initiate execution proceedings before the same Tribunal, and the offending vehicle can be attached as security.

4. **Limitation**: Pay-and-recover is available only to **third parties** (persons on the road or whose risk is statutorily covered). It is **not available** for gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles, persons travelling on prohibited parts of a vehicle (mud-guard), or passengers in private vehicles used for hire/reward — because these persons are not 'third parties' within the statutory scheme.

5. **Discretionary in some cases**: For passengers in goods vehicles (where the risk is not statutorily mandated), the appellate court has discretion to apply pay-and-recover depending on the facts, particularly the claimants' circumstances and the stage of litigation (*Ellappa*, doc_026).

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri

supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision that consolidates the entire law on pay-and-recover — the foundational authority in the corpus.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most authoritative judgment in the corpus on the principle. It resolves the earlier controversy about whether only the Supreme Court under Article 142 could order pay-and-recover, holding that Tribunals and High Courts also have this power.
supporting.quote: Even when the insurer has proved the breach on the part of the insured considering the policy condition and even if the said breach of condition is fundamental... the Tribunal can direct that the insurer make the payment and recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to satisfy a third-party award is statutory; it must pay first and recover from the owner/driver even if there is a breach of policy conditions such as an invalid driving licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: Invalid driving licence — the classic scenario for pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Clearly articulates that the liability is statutory and not contractual, tracing the principle from Skandia through Sohan Lal Passi to Swaran Singh.
supporting.quote: There is no manner of doubt that the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Where the driver lacks a valid driving licence (fundamental breach), the insurer must pay the third-party claimant first and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver without any valid licence — clearest case of fundamental breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Recent MACT decision (2024) applying the principle to a straightforward no-licence case, showing the principle remains current.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds an LMV licence without the specific endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner. The mode of recovery is per Nanjappan — execution in the same proceedings without a separate suit.
supporting.fact_alignment: Licence endorsement mismatch — driver had LMV licence but drove a heavy goods vehicle.
supporting.why_it_matters: Applies pay-and-recover to licence-class/endorsement issues and provides the procedural mechanism for recovery.
supporting.quote: The Tribunal can direct that the insurer is liable to be reimbursed by the insured for the compensation and other amounts which it has been compelled to pay to the third party under the award of the Tribunal.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where a transport vehicle driver holds only an LMV licence without the badge/authorisation for transport vehicles, the insurer must pay the claimant and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Transport vehicle driven without proper licence endorsement/badge.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends pay-and-recover to the specific context of transport vehicle licence requirements.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence had expired and was renewed more than 30 days later (so the renewal operates only from the date of renewal, not retrospectively), the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Lapsed/renewed licence — the accident occurred during the gap period.
supporting.why_it_matters: Applies pay-and-recover to the specific scenario of a lapsed licence renewed after the accident, clarifying that Section 15 of the MV Act does not give retrospective validity.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a driver lacks a special endorsement for transporting hazardous/dangerous goods under CMV Rules, the insurer is entitled to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Goods carriage carrying hazardous goods without the required special endorsement on the driving licence.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends pay-and-recover to hazardous goods transport — a niche but important application.

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Ellappa
supporting.principle: For passengers in goods vehicles (where risk is not statutorily required to be covered), pay-and-recover is not ipso facto applicable but may be applied discretionarily by the appellate court depending on facts — particularly the claimants' poverty and prolonged litigation.
supporting.fact_alignment: Passengers travelling in a goods vehicle — risk not covered under Section 147.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that pay-and-recover can be applied even outside the strict Section 149(4)/(5) framework, as a matter of judicial discretion in appropriate cases.
supporting.quote: In order to shorten the litigation and as the claimants, being the beneficiaries receiving the benefits flowing from the Motor Vehicles Act, a Social Welfare Legislation, are entitled to get their compensation without undergoing cumbersome legal proceedings, a direction of 'pay and recover' is inevitable.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a passenger is travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such a passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and the Tribunal cannot invoke pay-and-recover. The insurer is completely exonerated.
adverse.risk_to_client: Opposing counsel will cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is not available whenever the claimant is not a 'third party' in the strict statutory sense — e.g., passengers in private vehicles, unauthorised occupants.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is limited to its specific facts: a private jeep used for hire/reward (marriage party). It does not apply to standard third-party road users (pedestrians, other vehicle occupants) or to passengers whose risk is covered under the policy. The key distinction is whether the claimant is a 'third party' under Section 147 — a pedestrian or occupant of another vehicle always is.
adverse.quote: When the passenger travelling from the vehicle for hire or reward, against the policy condition, cannot be treated as 'third party'; then the Tribunal ought not to have passed the order of 'pay and recover' in this case.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where the risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the policy (gratuitous passengers in a goods vehicle), Sections 149(4) and (5) are not attracted, and neither the Tribunal nor the High Court has power to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: Opposing counsel will cite this to argue that pay-and-recover cannot be ordered for any category of claimant whose risk falls outside Section 147 — particularly gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles, tractors, etc.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case applies only where the risk is entirely outside the statutory coverage under Section 147. It does not apply where: (a) the risk is statutorily covered but there is a policy breach (licence defect), or (b) the claimant is a true third party (pedestrian, occupant of another vehicle). The distinction is between 'no coverage at all' vs 'coverage exists but there is a breach'.
adverse.quote: In cases where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the terms of the insurance policy... the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 149... are not attracted, and neither the Claims Tribunal nor the High Court has the power to direct the insurer to pay the compensation and recover it from the owner.

adverse.title: Dadapeera S/O Abdul Salam Sab vs Mallesh M S/O Hanumanthappa
adverse.principle: A person travelling on the mud-guard of a tractor violates Regulation 28 of the Rules of the Road Regulations and is not a 'third party' entitled to pay-and-recover. The insurer is exonerated.
adverse.risk_to_client: Opposing counsel will cite this to argue that any claimant who was on a prohibited part of a vehicle or travelling in violation of traffic regulations is not entitled to pay-and-recover.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turns on the specific prohibition under Regulation 28 against travelling on a tractor mud-guard — an inherently dangerous and illegal position. It does not apply to a claimant who was a pedestrian, a lawful passenger, or an occupant of another vehicle. The ratio is that the benefit of pay-and-recover is a statutory right of a 'third party', and a person violating safety regulations forfeits that status.
adverse.quote: The benefit of pay and recovery is a statutory benefit and protection given to the third party... In the present case, the claimant by sitting over mud-guard of tractor engine, cannot claim to be a third party.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy breaches such as an expired driving licence. The insurer can recover from the insured in the same proceedings.
adverse.risk_to_client: This is actually favourable to a claimant seeking pay-and-recover — it supports the principle. However, from an insurer's perspective, it is adverse because it confirms the insurer cannot escape liability to the third party even for licence expiry.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the pay-and-recover principle rather than limiting it. It is only 'adverse' from an insurer's perspective resisting payment. The case predates the Full Bench in Yallavva (doc_025) which is now the governing authority.

priority_arguments: Pay-and-recover is the settled statutory scheme under Sections 149(1), (4) and (5) of the MV Act, confirmed by the Full Bench in Yallavva (doc_025) — Tribunals and High Courts have the power to order it.
The insurer's liability to the third party is statutory, not contractual — it arises from the mere issuance of a certificate of insurance (Satto, doc_033).
Even fundamental breaches (no licence, expired licence, wrong licence class) do not absolve the insurer of liability to the third party — only the right to recover from the insured arises.
The mode of recovery is simple: execution in the same proceedings without a separate suit, per Nanjappan (cited in Chennamma, doc_027).
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a doctrinal question, not a quantum question.
risks: The opposing side will argue that the claimant is not a 'third party' (per Sukumarbai, doc_028; Minor Mahesh, doc_029; Dadapeera, doc_030) — this is the most dangerous argument and must be addressed head-on by establishing the claimant's status.
If the claimant was a gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle or on a prohibited part of a vehicle, pay-and-recover may be unavailable — the court has discretion but may refuse.
The insurer may argue that the breach was so fundamental that even pay-and-recover should not apply — though Yallavva (doc_025) holds this argument is not available for true third parties.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal under Section 166 of the MV Act. The claimant should seek a specific direction for pay-and-recover in the award itself, with liberty to the insurer to recover from the owner in the same proceedings.

caveats: This corpus does not contain the foundational Supreme Court judgments (Swaran Singh, Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Nanjappan) themselves — they are cited within the judgments but are not part of the 56-document corpus. The analysis here is based on how the corpus judgments apply those Supreme Court precedents.

Doc_034 (K.G. Srinivasamurthy) applies the principle implicitly (insurer liable despite expired licence, can recover) but does not use the phrase 'pay and recover' explicitly in its holding — it is included for completeness.
Doc_006 (National Insurance Co. v. Meena) mentions a pay-and-recover order in passing but its ratio focuses on contributory negligence — it is not a standalone authority on the principle.

payload.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
payload.holding: The Court held that while an attached trailer/trolley is part of an insured tractor and does not require separate insurance, the insurance company is absolved from liability because the tractor was being used to transport bricks and iron rods for construction rather than for agricultural purposes, violating the insurance policy terms.
payload.ratio: A trailer attached to a tractor is considered part of the tractor and does not require separate insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act; however, if the tractor is used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer is not liable to pay compensation.

args.question: Which judgments apply the 'pay and recover' principle, and in what circumstances?

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: The insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award even after proving a fundamental breach under Section 149(2), and may recover the amount from the insured. This applies to both Act policies and contractual policies. Tribunals and High Courts have the power to order pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision consolidating the entire law on pay-and-recover — the foundational authority in the corpus.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most authoritative judgment in the corpus. It resolves the earlier controversy about whether only the Supreme Court under Article 142 could order pay-and-recover, holding that Tribunals and High Courts also have this power.
supporting.quote: Even when the insurer has proved the breach on the part of the insured considering the policy condition and even if the said breach of condition is fundamental... the Tribunal can direct that the insurer make the payment and recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to satisfy a third-party award is statutory; it must pay first and recover from the owner/driver even if there is a breach of policy conditions such as an invalid driving licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: Invalid driving licence — the classic scenario for pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Clearly articulates that the liability is statutory and not contractual, tracing the principle from Skandia through Sohan Lal Passi to Swaran Singh.
supporting.quote: There is no manner of doubt that the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Where the driver lacks a valid driving licence (fundamental breach), the insurer must pay the third-party claimant first and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver without any valid licence — clearest case of fundamental breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Recent MACT decision (2024) applying the principle to a straightforward no-licence case, showing the principle remains current.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds an LMV licence without the specific endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner. The mode of recovery is per Nanjappan — execution in the same proceedings without a separate suit.
supporting.fact_alignment: Licence endorsement mismatch — driver had LMV licence but drove a heavy goods vehicle.
supporting.why_it_matters: Applies pay-and-recover to licence-class/endorsement issues and provides the procedural mechanism for recovery.
supporting.quote: The Tribunal can direct that the insurer is liable to be reimbursed by the insured for the compensation and other amounts which it has been compelled to pay to the third party under the award of the Tribunal.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where a transport vehicle driver holds only an LMV licence without the badge/authorisation for transport vehicles, the insurer must pay the claimant and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Transport vehicle driven without proper licence endorsement/badge.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends pay-and-recover to the specific context of transport vehicle licence requirements.
